title: Early-stage startups: act like a little company to win Early Adopters
summary: Jason argues that early-stage founders hurt themselves by posing as big, "professional" companies. Your next sale is an Early Adopter, not Lockheed Martin, so your public persona should be human, specific, and small-team, which attracts the customers who will actually help you build the right product.

principles.text: Your next sale won't be a big enterprise deal; early on you're mismatched with large companies.
principles.quote: My next sale won't be a 1000-seat order from Lockheed Martin.

principles.text: Early Adopters are the perfect match for a young product: they tolerate bugs and want a personal relationship with founders.
principles.quote: They don't mind putting up with a hundred bugs so long as they get fixed fast. They want to be involved in the process.

principles.text: Early Adopters take risks because new technology can give them a competitive advantage; most companies won't.
principles.quote: Most companies aren't willing to take risks for any reason, so this is a winning strategy for those willing to take risks.

principles.text: Early on you need engaged customers who help shape the product, not silent downloaders.
principles.quote: You don't need people who download, get discouraged, and then never call you back. You need a chatty Cathy who wants to dive in and help out.

principles.text: Write your site for the Early Adopter: expose your phone and Twitter, promote community over unbuilt features.
principles.quote: Should you hide behind "Contact Us" forms or display your phone number and Twitter account on your home page?

principles.text: Replace corporate marketing-speak with specific, human language.
principles.quote: Say something specific and meaningful. Be human. Be yourself.
